Title: The Raree Show! a Political Contrast to the Print of the Times, by Wm Hogarth
Producer name: After: Jefferyes Hamett O'Neale (in part);  Published by: Edward Sumpter
Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Lettered with the title, captions in the image, including 'The Full and Whole Play of Dido and Aeneas', four verses of four lines each 'See here my good Masters a fine Raree Show ... And acting each day in this Whimsical Nation' and scratched in upper right 'Price 1 Sh'.
Annotated in ink by Hawkins '[in the image] H. Fox / Hogarth / Bedford / Bute / Pss Wales / Smollett / [below the image] Bute / Churchill / Wandsworth Epist. See Gent Mag. 1762 p. 405. 441 / Beckford / Pitt / Temple / Newcastle / Cumberland / Whitfield / 176[2]'.;
Curators Comments:
Hogarth's "The Times Plate 1", published on 7 September 1762, supported moves to end the Seven Years War and was met by fierce attacks from those who feared that the treaty with France would result in the loss of territories and commercial opportunities gained. Sumpter was particularly active in producing opposition prints.
"The Wandsworth Epistle" was a letter supporting Bute written by an unknown person from Wandsworth and dated 5 September; it was widely circulated in the City of London. 
This is an early state before the insertion of Sumpter's publication line. It was advertised in the Public Advertiser, 8 October 1762, p.1, col.1: "This Day at Noon will be publish'd. Price One Shilling. A Political Contrast to the Historical Print of the Times By William Hogarth. In which is introduced a Group of new Characters, Foreign and Domestic. Sold by Edward Sumpter, at the Bible and Crown in Fleet Street.".
Sumpter advertised a  "Second Edition" on a broadside entitled "The Kitchen in an Uproar" (BM Satires 4043) published early in 1763. His publication line, and a price of sixpence, appears above the verses on several impressions in the BM; it was probably inserted at the time of this second edition. In impressions of this later state the earlier price of one shilling at top right can sometimes be read.
Certain elements of the design are close to the work of Jefferyes Hamett O'Neale: the lion is very similar to an example in the Ladies Amusement (first published by Sayer in 1760), and the group of Whitfield, his arms raised standing on a stool, with an animal-headed man beside him and a devil hovering above is close to BM Satire 4005, published by Sumpter on 2 May 1763.

Description: A collection of drawings and colour prints by William Dickes, mostly after his own designs. They vary considerably in size and subject and type; some are single sheet publications, others were sold in sets. The subjects include flowers, birds and animals,as well as portraits, religious subjects and landscape. c.1846-1873 (mostly);
Producer name: Print made by: William Dickes
Dimensions: 290.00 millimetres Sheet of 'Autumn Fruits' ;  337.00 millimetres Sheet of 'Autumn Fruits' ;
Curators Comments:
The collection was bequeathed through the NACF by Alfred Docker, the author of the standard catalogue of Dickes' prints, published in 1924. The collection is partly kept mounted (in two volumes) and partly loose (in two portfolios). The register follows the order of the Docker catalogue, and includes the preparatory drawings (when Docker had managed to acquire them) in the same sequence as the related prints. All the drawings (unless they were oversize) and the related prints have been extracted and mounted together in two albums; the sequence within the albums is neither that of the register nor of the Docker catalogue. The outsize drawings plus all the remaining prints have been placed in two portfolios, arranged in the order of the Docker catalogue. 
The entire collection has the register numbers 1931,0213.1 to 1379. The entries on the database give two overlapping entries, one for the albums, the other for the portfolios; the first and last numbers in the sequence assigned to each are those in that location. These cover the numbers 1 to 1315.  From 1316 to the end the items have individual entries and locations. A few individual entries in the range from 1 to 1315 have been created for items kept in other locations.
